options: The model thinking harmful thoughts
The model responding too quickly
Using more than one AI model in an app
Giving an LLM-based system too much power — too many tools, too much permission, or too much autonomy to act without a check — so a wrong or hijacked model can do real damage

explain.right: Excessive agency is about what the system can DO: the more it can act unchecked, the bigger the blast radius when it's wrong or hijacked.
explain.wrong: It's not about the model's 'thoughts', its speed, or model count — it's about excessive capability to act.

items.q: A summarizer feature has been given a tool that can delete files, though it never needs to. Why is that a problem, and what's the fix?
options: No problem — it only matters if the tool is actually used
Add more tools so it has options
Fix it by telling the model in the prompt not to delete files
The capability itself is the risk; apply least privilege (remove the tool) and keep a human on consequential actions

explain.right: A capability the feature doesn't need is pure attack surface; remove it (least privilege) and gate consequential actions behind a human.
explain.wrong: The unused power is still exploitable; a prompt instruction isn't a security boundary, and more tools means more risk.

items.q: Which practice best prevents an LLM app from disclosing one user's data to another (LLM02)?
options: Ask users politely not to request others' data
Enforce access control before data reaches the model, so a user's agent can only ever retrieve that user's own rows
Make the model's answers shorter
Tell the model in the system prompt to keep each user's data private

explain.right: Filter data to the current user at the data layer before it enters the context; then even a prompt injection can't make the model fetch someone else's rows.
explain.wrong: A system-prompt instruction is not a security boundary, politeness isn't a control, and answer length is irrelevant.

items.q: What is the key lesson of 'system prompt leakage' (LLM07)?
options: The system prompt can be extracted, so never place secrets in it — treat anything in it as potentially discoverable
Leakage only happens if you share your prompt publicly
System prompts should always be shown to users
The system prompt is a secure vault, so put API keys in it

explain.right: System prompts can be coaxed out, so they're not a safe place for secrets; keep credentials in the environment and behind tools instead.
explain.wrong: It's not a vault, it needn't be public, and the risk exists regardless of whether you deliberately shared it.

items.q: In a retrieval (RAG) app, an attacker uploads a document full of hidden instructions into the knowledge base. Which two LLM risks are in play?
options: Only misinformation (LLM09)
None — RAG is immune to injection
Vector/embedding weaknesses (LLM08) and indirect prompt injection (LLM01) — the poisoned document becomes instructions when retrieved
Only unbounded consumption (LLM10)

explain.right: Poisoned retrieval stores (LLM08) feed indirect injection (LLM01) when the document is retrieved and read as instructions; partition and vet what gets embedded.
explain.wrong: It's more than consumption or misinformation, and RAG is very much exposed to injection via retrieved content.
